results.result: Hair-bundle stiffness increases along the tonotopic axis of the rat cochlea, with outer hair cells showing steeper gradients (240% increase over 1-4 kHz) than inner hair cells (240% increase over 1-15 kHz). At each cochlear position, outer hair-cell bundles were stiffer than inner hair-cell bundles, with the stiffness ratio increasing from apex to base.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C27-C30, C35-C36, C98-C99 collectively demonstrate stiffness gradients along the tonotopic axis with statistical support (p<0.05) and quantitative measurements from force-displacement relations (Figure 2). The data show consistent trends across multiple cochlear locations with adequate sample sizes (n=11-21 per location).

results.result: The gating-spring stiffness shows intrinsic gradients along the tonotopic axis that exceed predictions based on morphology alone. Between 1-4 kHz, gating-spring stiffness increased by 520% for outer hair cells and 300% for inner hair cells. Measured stiffness ratios were ~50% and ~70% larger than morphologically predicted for outer and inner hair cells, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C87, C91-C92 are supported by dissection of hair-bundle mechanics into gating-spring and pivot contributions (Figure 3). The comparison between measured and morphologically predicted stiffness ratios provides strong evidence for intrinsic mechanical gradients beyond morphological effects.

results.result: Tip-link disruption by EDTA iontophoresis revealed resting tension in hair bundles at all cochlear locations tested. Hair-bundle tension showed a steep gradient for outer hair cells (13-fold increase from 18±7 pN to 248±59 pN, 1-4 kHz) but a weaker gradient for inner hair cells (3.3-fold increase from 24±5 pN to 100±22 pN, 1-15 kHz).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by systematic measurements of positive bundle offsets upon tip-link disruption (Figure 5A-B) with statistical significance (p<0.01 for outer hair cells, p<0.05 comparing gradients). Sample sizes are adequate (n=12-71 per group) and the method is validated by concurrent stiffness decrease and channel closure.

results.result: Single tip-link tension shows gradients along the tonotopic axis independent of tip-link number. At 1 kHz, single tip-link tension was comparable between cell types (~5-6 pN). At 4 kHz, tension increased by 620% to 34±8 pN in outer hair cells but only 170% to 16±4 pN in inner hair cells, with statistically steeper gradients for outer hair cells (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 demonstrate that tension gradients persist at the single tip-link level after accounting for tip-link number (Figure 5C). The calculation methodology is clearly described, combining bundle tension measurements with tip-link counts and geometric factors. Statistical validation confirms steeper gradients in outer hair cells.

results.result: EDTA iontophoresis evoked biphasic hair-bundle movements: an initial negative deflection associated with increased inward current, followed by positive movement upon tip-link disruption. The negative movement is explained by increased gating-spring tension at reduced extracellular Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C132, C136 are supported by simultaneous mechanical and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4). The biphasic response is consistently observed (n=101 inner, n=44 outer hair cells) and the interpretation within the gating-spring model framework is mechanistically sound and consistent with established theory.

results.result: Maximal tip-link tension before disruption showed gradients from 14±4 pN to 54±12 pN (1-4 kHz) in outer hair cells and 15±3 pN to 44±8 pN (1-4 kHz) in inner hair cells. In higher Ca2+ (500 µM), negative movements were reversible and reached steady-state, suggesting Ca2+-dependent modulation of resting tip-link tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 are supported by measurements at the peak of negative deflection (Figure 6) with adequate sample sizes (n=23-49 per group). The reversibility experiments in 500 µM Ca2+ (n=6 preparations) provide additional evidence for Ca2+-dependent tension regulation, though the smaller sample size for reversibility is noted.

results.result: Rotational stiffness of stereociliary pivots showed limited variation along the tonotopic axis. For inner hair cells, no significant variation was observed between 1-2 kHz or 4-15 kHz locations, though a 100% increase occurred between 2-4 kHz. Pivot stiffness gradients are entirely determined by morphology, unlike intact bundle stiffness.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C93 are supported by measurements after tip-link disruption (Figure 3C). The finding that pivot stiffness gradients match morphological predictions while intact bundle gradients exceed them provides strong evidence for intrinsic mechanical regulation at the tip-link complex level.

results.result: The authors conclude that mechanical gradients of the tip-link complex may help specify the characteristic frequency of the hair cell, particularly for outer hair cells in an active resonance framework where the stiffness gradient could be steep enough to be a major determinant of the tonotopic map.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C89, C108, C157 represent speculative conclusions about functional significance. While the measured gradients are well-supported, the causal link to frequency tuning is not directly tested. The authors acknowledge uncertainty about the exact contribution of hair bundles to frequency tuning (C153) and note that measurements were limited to the apical half of the cochlea.

results.result: Force-displacement relations were remarkably linear with no sign of gating compliance. This is attributed to either the rise time (~500 µs) being too long to outspeed fast adaptation, or gating forces being too weak under the experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39, C150 are supported by the linear force-displacement data (Figure 2B,D) and consistent with previous fluid-jet studies (citations provided). The authors provide two plausible mechanistic explanations supported by literature, though they cannot definitively distinguish between them.

results.result: Hair bundles showed mechanical creep during force steps (22% for inner hair cells, 12% for outer hair cells), which was strongly reduced upon tip-link disruption by EDTA. This creep is attributed to mechanical relaxation of tip-link tension associated with myosin-based adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by force-step responses (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5) showing consistent creep behavior that is abolished by tip-link disruption. The interpretation is consistent with established adaptation mechanisms, though the molecular basis is not directly tested.

results.result: Experiments were performed on juvenile rats (P7-P10) before hearing onset, with 92% of recordings at P8 or later. The tip-link complex is expected to be nearly mature at these ages, at least in outer hair cells, though maturation progresses base-to-apex and may affect gradient estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 accurately describe the experimental conditions and acknowledge potential developmental confounds. The inference about maturity is supported by citations to developmental studies, though the authors appropriately note uncertainty about inner hair cell maturation at apical locations.

results.result: The authors propose that tip-link tension gradients may compensate for conductance gradients to maintain uniform channel open probability (~0.5) along the tonotopic axis in outer hair cells. Higher tension at basal locations would counteract the closing effect of increased Ca2+ influx from higher conductance channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C114 present a compensatory mechanism hypothesis supported by literature on conductance gradients and Ca2+ effects. However, this is speculative integration of the current findings with prior work rather than direct experimental validation. The uniform open probability (C110) is from a cited study, not measured here.

results.result: Tip-link tension is thought to be produced by molecular motors, and the observed tension gradient implies more motors or higher motor forces at basal locations. Inner hair cells showed less tension than outer hair cells, consistent with their lower channel open probability and weaker conductance gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 logically connect the measured tension gradients to motor mechanisms (supported by citations) and to known differences between inner and outer hair cells. The comparative analysis is well-supported by the data (Figure 5B-C), though the molecular motor mechanism is not directly tested.

results.result: The measured tip-link tensions are compatible with molecular dynamics predictions about PCDH15 bending elasticity at low frequencies/apex, but may exceed the threshold for EC9-10 unbending (~10 pN per filament) or even EC domain unfolding at higher frequencies/more basal locations, potentially contributing to stiffness gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C127 integrate the measured tensions with molecular structure predictions from simulations. While the comparison is informative, it relies on assumptions about PCDH15 dimerization and equal tension sharing that are not directly validated. The speculation about domain unfolding (C126) is acknowledged as such.

results.result: Gating-spring tension gradients were associated with stiffness gradients, potentially explained by strain stiffening of macromolecules like PCDH15, or alternatively by variable numbers of compliant molecules operating in parallel.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 present mechanistic hypotheses for the observed correlation between tension and stiffness gradients. While strain stiffening is a well-established phenomenon (C129), the specific application to explain the observed gradients is speculative. Alternative mechanisms (C131) are also proposed without direct evidence.

results.result: The increase in tip-link tension at reduced Ca2+ could result from increased motor force or from gating-spring stiffening/shortening. The motor mechanism is favored because slow adaptation was observed, which would counteract steady-state tension changes from gating-spring property changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 present competing mechanistic explanations for Ca2+-dependent tension changes, with the authors favoring the motor mechanism based on the observation of slow adaptation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). The logic is sound, though the alternative membrane mechanics hypothesis (C140-C141) cannot be definitively ruled out.

results.result: Hair bundles can operate in two regimes: one dominated by gating forces (positive movements upon depolarization) and another dominated by resting tension changes (negative movements, as observed here). The two regimes can coexist if gating forces are strong enough, but gating forces were weak in this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C149 reconcile apparently contradictory findings from different studies through a two-regime framework supported by citations. The interpretation is consistent with the linear force-displacement relations observed (indicating weak gating forces) and with prior work in other species showing bidirectional responses.

results.result: If stiffness gradients continued toward more basal locations, the base-to-apex ratio would be ~40 for outer hair cells (comparable to the frequency range 0.5-50 kHz) but only ~6 for inner hair cells. For passive spring-mass resonance, two orders of magnitude in frequency would require a 10,000-fold stiffness increase, much steeper than observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101, C104 involve hypothetical extrapolations beyond the measured cochlear region. While the calculations are mathematically sound, they assume linear continuation of gradients that were only measured over a limited range. The comparison to passive resonance requirements (C104) is valid but the authors acknowledge this mechanism is unlikely.

results.result: In an active resonance framework based on spontaneous oscillations, the characteristic frequency is set by oscillator frequency, which increases with hair-bundle stiffness. The relation may be steeper than passive spring-mass systems, possibly approximating linear dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 present an alternative theoretical framework supported by citations, but this is speculative discussion rather than tested hypothesis. The authors use this framework to argue their measured gradients could be functionally relevant, but do not provide direct evidence for active resonance in their preparation.

results.result: Stiffness and tension gradients were steeper for outer hair cells than inner hair cells, reflecting the division of labor where outer hair cells serve as mechanical amplifiers. This may impose more stringent regulatory constraints on outer hair cells to tune their mechanoreceptive antenna.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C152 summarize the comparative findings (Figures 2E, 5B) and provide functional interpretation consistent with established roles of the two cell types. The interpretation is reasonable though the causal link between division of labor and gradient steepness is inferential.

results.result: Hair-bundle morphology is not the sole determinant of hair-bundle mechanics.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is directly supported by the finding that measured stiffness gradients exceed morphologically predicted gradients (C91), demonstrating intrinsic mechanical regulation beyond structural changes. This is a key conclusion enabling the identification of tip-link complex contributions.

results.result: Recordings were made at four cochlear locations (1, 2, 4, 15 kHz) corresponding to 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50% distance from the apex of the typically 10-mm rat cochlea. Both inner and outer hair cells were measured at 1-4 kHz, but only inner hair cells at 15 kHz. The fluid-jet pipette was positioned ~8 µm from the hair bundle.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22, C159-C161 describe the experimental design and are supported by Figure 1 and the Materials and methods section. These are straightforward methodological details that are clearly documented.
